links.note: When the inauguration day was - 10 May 1994, the day the first democratic non-racial government was installed. 24136 is that day.
The date of the inauguration - the historical moment 24136 records.
What the nation still needed liberating from - poverty, deprivation and gender discrimination. The freedom of all his people, not his own.
The meaning of 'emancipation' as used in 'We have achieved our political emancipation' - inferring a word from its sentence, which is 24148.
The colours of the new South African flag, trailed by the jets - part of the ceremony's symbolism in 24143.
The colours of the new flag shown in the flypast - the ceremony's symbolic display.
Why two national anthems were sung - unity and the end of racial discrimination. A symbolic act of the ceremony.
Why two national anthems were sung - the ceremony's symbolism of a shared, non-racial state.
Whom Mandela wished to thank but could not - the African patriots who no longer existed. The cost of decades of oppression.
Whom he wanted to thank but could not - the patriots whose suffering and courage could never be repaid.
A man's obligations in life - to his family and to his people. The turn from personal to collective freedom in 24146.
A man's twin obligations, to family and to people - the widening of his hunger for freedom.
Which party Mandela joined - the African National Congress, the step his hunger for his people's freedom led to.
Who is not free according to Mandela - both oppressor and oppressed. His conception of freedom for all.
Whether there is colour prejudice in our own country, with the verse ending 'you have the cheek to call me coloured' - about race-based separation, which is 24138.
Why other countries broke off diplomatic relations with South Africa - the apartheid policy. 24138 is that system.
What structure Mandela means by 'one of the harshest, most inhumane societies' - racial domination against the dark-skinned. That is apartheid.
What created a lasting wound in his country - the policy of apartheid. 24138 exactly.
Where the ceremonies took place - the sandstone amphitheatre at the Union Buildings, on the day of the installation.
Where the ceremonies took place and comparable sandstone buildings in India - the setting of the historical day.
How 10 May is an autumn day in South Africa - a fact about the date of the installation.
What ceremonies took place on 10 May - Mandela sworn in as first black president after three centuries of white rule.
How Mandela became the first black president - the first democratic elections and 252 of 400 seats. The historical moment.
Which flame can be hidden but never extinguished - man's goodness. A figurative expression Mandela uses, which is 24149.
What the military generals do and how their attitude changed - they saluted and pledged loyalty. 24143 is that salute as a sign of the new order.
Why two national anthems were sung - each group sang its own. The ceremony's symbolism.
Why two national anthems were sung - unity and the end of racial discrimination, a symbolic act of the day.
What the Impala jets' smoke trail symbolised - the new South African flag. The ceremony's symbolism.
What courage means to Mandela - not the absence of fear but the triumph over it, learnt from comrades in the struggle.
Whether loving or hating is natural - his conclusion drawn from decades of oppression, that goodness cannot be extinguished.
Why it is easy to learn to love - because it comes naturally. His reflection after the years of racial domination.
What he means by being 'simply the sum of all those African patriots' - the courage the decades of oppression produced.
A country's greatest wealth - its people, finer than the purest diamonds, from whom he learnt courage.
The greatest wealth of a nation - its people, whose courage under oppression the passage goes on to describe.
Defining courage, given that Mandela calls it the triumph over fear - the courage oppression produced in his comrades.
What pained him on becoming president - that he could not thank the patriots who had died. The cost of the long oppression.
The twin obligations - to family and to people, community and country. The widening of freedom in 24146.
Whether the oppressor is free - no, he is a prisoner of hatred. Mandela's account of freedom for all.
Two ways oppressor and oppressed are alike - both robbed of their humanity. The freedom-for-all argument.
What Mandela thought of oppressor and oppressed - both must be liberated. 24146's conception of freedom.
